rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.6 and 3 - own field experiment in a Fuji apple orchard at Prosser, WA, 2013 season, seven automatic scheduling treatments in a randomized complete block design with three replicates. Q2: Abstract, Section 3.1, Table 2, Fig. 7, Conclusions - automatic plant-based (TTT, CWSI) and weather-based (WB) algorithms applied the same water as the neutron-probe benchmark, cut applied water by about 70% versus conventional practice, kept stem water potential in the non-stressed range and soil water deficit below MAD; authors state preliminary results support automatic management of drip-irrigated apple trees. Q3: Section 2.3 and Fig. 7a/7b - plant status confirmed by two independent methods, pressure-bomb midday stem water potential and neutron-probe soil water deficit, plus field inspection of tree condition. Q4: Fig. 7a and 7b - intermediate variables (root-zone soil water deficit and stem water potential) measured weekly under the automatic treatments. Q7: Section 3.3 - from the field experience, regular cleaning/maintenance of IRTs is stated as necessary to keep the plant-based network running; for soil-sensor algorithms, site-specific calibration and more sensors are stated as necessary (Table 4, Section 3.3). Q8: Section 3.2 and Conclusions - trees in an alternate-bearing year so no quantitative yield data collected; results described as preliminary, initial step, single season; system only operational from June after rain and perched water table; sensors not calibrated. Q9: Table 2 - SE of mean reported for total applied water per treatment; Fig. 7 error bars show SE of soil water deficit and stem water potential.
rows.notes: The study supports improved irrigation management (water saving while maintaining non-stressed plant water status) but did not measure yield or fruit quality quantitatively; crop production support is only qualitative observations of tree growth and fruit size. Single orchard, single soil, single season.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.6 - own field experiment in an apple orchard, 2013, with a soil-tension (Watermark granular matrix sensor) threshold treatment (SOIL) among seven treatments. Q2: Table 2 and Section 3.1 - SOIL applied the lowest total water (214 mm, 53% of NP, 16% of conventional), significantly less than all other treatments; Section 3.1 and Abstract report this came with tangible under-irrigation and stress symptoms. Q4: Fig. 6 and Section 2.4.2 - soil water potential readings from the Watermark sensors (the variable triggering and stopping irrigation) were logged and shown to stay within 0 to -80 kPa, explaining why little water was applied; applied water logged per plot. Q8: Section 3.1 and 3.3 - sensors were not field-calibrated, single predefined thresholds applied to all, one sensor per plot sampling a limited soil volume possibly away from active roots, difficulty of representative tension measurement under heterogeneous drip wetting; single season preliminary study. Q9: Table 2 - SE of mean for SOIL applied water (32 mm); Fig. 6 shows SE of mean of sensor readings.
rows.notes: Applied water measured by one method only (irrigation records), so no triangulation. Authors state that site-specific calibration, more sensors, or combined potential/content sensors appear necessary for the soil-based method to be accurate, but this is stated as a condition for avoiding under-irrigation rather than for the water reduction itself, so Q7 rated no. Watermark sensors are granular matrix sensors rather than tensiometers, but they are soil matric potential sensors, so technology matches.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.6 - own orchard field experiment with the SOIL (Watermark threshold) treatment. Q2: Abstract, Sections 3.1 and 3.2 - SOIL and SL+WB plots showed leaf drop, loss of turgidity, reduced shoot and foliage growth, shorter trees, and abnormally small fruits that never ripened compared with conventional plots; authors conclude soil-based approaches failed to deliver enough water, causing severe water stress and impaired growth (Conclusions). Q4: Table 2 and Fig. 6 - applied water (214 mm, lowest) and the sensor soil water potential readings that governed irrigation were measured, and under-irrigation is identified as the pathway to stress. Q7: Section 3.3 and Table 4 - from their own results, authors state that site-specific calibration of individual sensors, a larger number of sensors, or combined potential and content sensors appears necessary for the soil-based method to deliver enough water; Section 3.1 attributes the harm to uncalibrated sensors with single thresholds sampling a limited soil volume. Q8: Section 3.2 - alternate bearing year so no quantitative yield data, only observations; Section 3.1 - sensors uncalibrated, one sensor per plot, stress in SL+WB described as 'may have been'; stem water potential and neutron probe not measured in SOIL plots.
rows.notes: The stress and fruit-quality harm is based on qualitative field observation only; the Watermark readings themselves showed no stress, and no pressure-bomb or neutron probe data were collected in SOIL plots, so no triangulation and no dispersion measure for the harm result. Fruit quality was not quantified (fruit size noted as noticeably smaller, unripened).

notes: Full text available including tables and figure captions. Single orchard, single soil (Warden silt loam), single season (2013) in semi-arid central Washington; yield not quantified because of alternate bearing year.
